title: Player Guide: the Sixty Interest Groups
issuedBy: Assembly Information Service — orientation for prospective players
sourceRef: World Bible v3.4, § 17 and Appendix B
summary: An introduction for prospective players to the electorate: six voter families, sixty publicly described groups, the five axes on which they judge parties, and the wider political currents they overlap with.

sections.heading: Who votes
paragraphs: The world’s adult human population — about 9.16 billion people in 2040 — votes in twelve regions for the 600-seat Assembly: 300 constituency seats and 300 global-list seats that bring each party’s total close to its share of the world vote (a party needs two per cent to qualify).

The electorate is modelled as **sixty voter groups in six families**. Every family appears in every region, in different proportions. Groups are simulated actors with standing profiles, budgets and consistent histories; they are not invented on the spot to reward or punish anyone.
Almost every voter has a powerful AI adviser. That improves factual understanding but leaves value differences intact — misleading persuasion, unequal access and strategic voting are still real.

sections.heading: The five axes
paragraphs: Every group has a position on each axis and gives each axis a different weight. A party is scored by how close it is to a group on the axes that group cares about most.

sections.heading: The six families
paragraphs: Families describe recurring political motivations, not classes of people, and they are **not** the founding parties. A party can draw on several families, and two groups in one family can disagree on nearly every practical bill.

sections.heading: Settlers — claim, settlement and early action
paragraphs: *Divided over:* speed, territorial priority, acceptable risks and who receives claims.

rows: Frontier Pioneers
Would-be founders of distant autonomous settlements. Demand early site access and meaningful self-government; resist indefinite moratoria.
Probe Lobbyists
Manufacturers, engineers and investors tied to interstellar mission chains. Favour legal certainty for launched missions; can switch parties over compensation and safety standards.
Homestead Migrants
Households seeking independent titles in newly accessible systems. Support individually transferable claims but oppose concentration by incumbent firms.
Industrial Expanders
Operators and beneficiaries of self-reproducing industrial capacity. Favour early allocation to industrial seeds and infrastructure; resist prohibitions with unclear scope.
Planetary Colonists
People seeking long-duration settlements on planetary surfaces. Demand habitable-site protections, safe terraforming and stable local law.
Risk Acceptors
People who value ambitious experiments and fast exploration. Tolerate higher exploratory risks but object to concealed external harms and coercion.
Legacy Builders
Families and communities seeking projects that last for generations. Support durable endowments and visible works; may back reserves linked to named future beneficiaries.
Claim-First Loyalists
Partisans of early missions and first-possession doctrines. Defend prior claims and could mobilise against retroactive curtailments.
Speed Pragmatists
Supporters of technically feasible, staged expansion. Value deployment schedules and measurable results; abandon slogans unsupported by capacity.
Rapid Distributors
Advocates of putting released claims into use promptly. Support fast releases but split between individual distribution and common development.

sections.heading: Stewards — protection and conservation
paragraphs: *Divided over:* permanent bans versus limited, carefully monitored settlement.

rows: Preserve Keepers
Administrators and supporters of protected cosmic environments. Want binding sanctuaries and penalties for destruction; insist on clear boundaries.
Near-Space Settlers
People favouring modest exploration near Earth and nearby stars. Accept regulated settlement but oppose distant irreversible commitments.
Wilderness Advocates
Believers in the intrinsic value of unmodified environments. Defend unvisited systems from industrial conversion, even where no human would be harmed.
Ecological Guardians
Researchers and campaigners concerned with alien or emergent ecologies. Require precautionary surveys before engineering potentially living worlds.
Cautious Neighbors
Communities worried that others’ expansion imposes shared risks. Prioritise externality controls, consultation and enforceable liability.
Heritage Protectors
Associations defending historic places, artefacts and inherited landscapes. Prefer preservation covenants; object to projects that erase culturally important records.
Observers’ Bloc
Scientists and contemplative groups preferring study before intervention. Support observatories and non-invasive missions; can back long-term restraint.
Minimal-Footprint Colonists
Settlers committed to low-impact human presence. Support habitation where footprints are limited and monitored.
Intergenerational Stewards
Advocates for the option value of untouched resources. Favour reserves and periodic review over irreversible present-day decisions.
Slow Settlers
Advocates of expansion conditional on accumulated knowledge. Can support eventual settlement if scientific triggers and sunset reviews are credible.

sections.heading: Holders — individual title and trading
paragraphs: *Divided over:* free markets versus family, community and waiting-period restrictions.

rows: Equal-Share Traders
People whose central concern is universal initial ownership. Want equal, enforceable shares; resist privileged allocations to incumbents.
Open-Exchange Holders
Owners who regard liquid trading as essential to autonomy. Oppose transfer restrictions; favour transparent competitive markets.
Kin Holders
Households managing shares through families and descendants. Demand reliable inheritance, guardianship and protection against fraud.
Share Speculators
Investors accepting risk in future resource claims. Favour liquid markets, predictable titles and disclosure; react strongly to retroactive changes.
Community Holders
Cooperatives and local associations pooling individual endowments. Support voluntary collective title; oppose compulsory collectivisation.
Private Ventures
Entrepreneurs combining resource rights with industrial projects. Favour stable contracts and entrepreneurial access over monopoly concessions.
Pledge Givers
People who commit their shares to charitable or moral causes. Demand robust trusts and commitments enforceable beyond a holder’s lifetime.
Waiting-Period Holders
Supporters of temporary limits on immediate sale. Favour cooling-off periods and anti-manipulation rules without permanent paternalism.
Anti-Pooling Holders
Critics of compulsory pooled institutions. Resist mandatory trusts and legislative diversion of individual rights.
Direct-Use Holders
People wanting to use their own shares for concrete projects. Want accessible project tools; dislike systems where only large companies can build.

sections.heading: Builders — public goods and common projects
paragraphs: *Divided over:* technocratic planning versus participatory control.

rows: Public Works Builders
Coalitions favouring shared interstellar infrastructure. Back relays, surveys and common utilities funded through Assembly projects.
Research Funders
Supporters of openly tested science. Want independent verification and publication rather than corporate capture.
Shared-Sky Advocates
People who see cosmic resources as a common inheritance. Favour broad public benefit; disagree on central planning versus community control.
Moral Project Funders
Donors and organisers prioritising ethical objectives. Back projects justified by welfare or rights rather than sheer output.
Long-Term Trustees
Supporters of fiduciary institutions that endure for centuries. Want auditability, trustee-removal rules and protection from political raids.
Civic Councils
Local and regional democratic institutions seeking a role in implementation. Demand participation, fiscal transparency and local autonomy.
Regional Commons
Coalitions worried that powerful regions monopolise common investment. Push geographic fairness across the twelve regions.
Infrastructure Planners
Logistics, energy and engineering communities. Prefer coherent sequences of investment over symbolic announcements.
Mutual Benefit Pools
Associations coordinating cross-group public goods. Support bargains with measurable benefits to several constituencies.
Assembly Loyalists
Voters who identify common projects with parliamentary legitimacy. Defend Assembly authority; oppose informal Council or corporate substitutes.

sections.heading: Inclusionists — future and digital persons and an enlarged franchise
paragraphs: *Divided over:* which minds or future persons deserve representation, and on what terms.

rows: Later-Generation Advocates
Supporters of political consideration for people not yet born. Demand reserved resources and limits on irreversible depletion.
Digital Rights Advocates
Campaigners for persistent artificial persons. Press for due process, protection from deletion and recognition beyond property law.
Emulation Families
Kin and partners of uploaded or copied persons. Defend continuity of marriage, inheritance and family status across substrates.
Agent Operators
People responsible for persistent agents. Seek clear duties and safeguards; divided over operators’ versus agents’ rights.
Youth Cohort
Young and soon-to-be-enfranchised people worried about inherited commitments. Demand generational accountability and ways to revise earlier settlements.
Universal Franchise
Maximal advocates of political inclusion. Support broad voting eligibility but must answer duplication and identity verification.
Sentience Advocates
Campaigners for potentially conscious animals and AIs. Prefer precautionary welfare protection where consciousness is uncertain.
Copy-Limit Reformers
People concerned with the rights and electoral effects of replication. Support limits or safeguards on copying; disagree over consent and identity.
Representation Reformers
Electoral designers seeking institutions beyond territorial suffrage. Explore chambers, trustees or weighted representation.
Cautious Inclusionists
Reformers wanting evidence before wholesale franchise change. Support welfare rights first and reviewable enfranchisement later.

sections.heading: Deferrers — delay and delegation for reflection
paragraphs: *Divided over:* human deliberation versus delegated AI inquiry and authority.

rows: Reflection First
Voters who put moral deliberation before irreversible action. Favour smaller early releases and serious inquiry commitments.
Council Delegators
Supporters of deliberation by aligned AI delegates. Want transparent delegation and appeal routes, not unlimited machine sovereignty.
Moral Realists
People who believe correct moral answers may be discoverable. Fund rigorous moral research and update as evidence improves.
Research Patrons
Financiers of long-term foundational inquiry. Back science that reduces uncertainty before cosmic-scale spending.
Wait-and-See Centrists
Uncommitted voters suspicious of rapid institutional commitments. Prefer reversible pilots and clear reporting.
Philosophers’ Bloc
Academic and public communities in normative debate. Demand pluralistic argument; resist treating forecasts as moral verdicts.
Verification Hawks
Citizens sceptical of unverifiable AI guarantees. Back independent audits, constrained delegation and adversarial safety reviews.
Slow Constitutionalists
Supporters of durable constitutional procedure. Favour high thresholds, staged amendments and protection against deadline crises.
Arbiter Reliants
People who rely on consistent legal administration. Value precedent and transparent adjudication; distrust personalised exceptions.
Uncertainty Hedgers
Groups prioritising resilience across very different futures. Prefer diversified investments and reserves over one irreversible bet.

sections.heading: How groups behave
list: Support moves with enacted policy, welfare and legal conditions, world events, press coverage and organised advocacy.
Groups can endorse, withhold support, split, bargain or change priorities when the world changes — but not without a reason such as new leadership, incentives or evidence.
Close scores split a group’s support between parties; regions draw on different mixtures of groups, so a regional campaign is a different campaign.
Moderators publish noisy *family-level* polling each term. Each party may commission two *subgroup* polls per term.
A promise to a family is not a guarantee of its votes.

sections.heading: Wider currents
paragraphs: Earth politics continues beside the treaty: nations still govern domestic law and the Grand Bargain still binds. With welfare no longer tied to wages, the old arguments over ownership have moved to who controls self-reproducing industry and cosmic claims.

*Illustrative.* The World Bible names no such movements. Most voters belong to one group and sympathise with several currents. Currents play no part in election results, which score groups only on the five axes, and say nothing about any group’s hidden loyalties.

sections.heading: What is not published
paragraphs: The groups’ salience weights, loyalty, turnout, regional weights and the simulation’s random draws stay in the moderators’ model. Strategy should be intelligible from public information, not reverse-engineered from hidden numbers. These descriptions are segments of a simulated electorate, not real organisations, and none is affiliated automatically with any party. See also the [[DOC-ELECTORATE|Public Electorate Reference]] and the six party guides.
